content_html:
Embodied mind

The embodied mind is a concept that sits at the crossroads of philosophy, neuroscience, cognitive science, and Buddhism. It emerged as a response to overly abstract, computational models of cognition.

  • Cognition arises through brain–body–environment loops
  • Meaning and memory are situated, enacted, relational
  • The “self” is empty of inherent essence but emerges through embodiment and interaction

It’s a bridge concept: modern cognitive science meets Buddhist insights about non-duality and impermanence.

Against “disembodied” cognition

Early cognitive science (1950s–80s): saw the mind as an abstract computer — symbol manipulation, independent of body or environment. Embodied cognition challenges this: thinking cannot be separated from the body that perceives, moves, and acts. Body is constitutive, not just a vessel: The body doesn’t just carry the brain; bodily structure and capacities shape how we think. Cognition emerges in interaction with the environment — not in isolation. Concepts are built from bodily experiences (e.g., “grasping an idea” stems from literal grasping).

Mind is not “inside” the skull alone but arises from feedback loops of brain–body–world.

  • Perception and action share circuits (mirror neurons, sensorimotor cortex).
  • Imagining an action activates similar brain areas as performing it.
  • Memory, reasoning, and even language draw on embodied simulations.

Philosophy / Complexity

  • Phenomenology (Merleau-Ponty): Consciousness is always being-in-the-world, not detached observation.
  • Enactivism: Cognition is enacted through activity; meaning is not pre-given but arises in lived interaction.
  • Complex systems: Mind is emergent — not in neurons alone, but in patterns of relation (similar to ecosystems).

Buddhist influence

The Embodied Mind* explicitly links cognitive science with Buddhist philosophy. Both traditions stress:

  • The self is not a fixed entity but arises in dependent origination.
  • Experience is shaped by attention, context, and practice.

Mind is process, not substance.

References

  • Varela, F. J., Thompson, E., & Rosch, E. (1991). The Embodied Mind: Cognitive Science and Human Experience. MIT Press.
  • Merleau-Ponty, M. (1962). Phenomenology of Perception. Routledge.
  • Lakoff, G., & Johnson, M. (1999). Philosophy in the Flesh: The Embodied Mind and Its Challenge to Western Thought. Basic Books.
  • Thompson, E. (2007). Mind in Life: Biology, Phenomenology, and the Sciences of Mind. Harvard University Press.
  • Schacter, D. L. (1999). The seven sins of memory: Insights from psychology and cognitive neuroscience. American Psychologist, 54(3), 182–203. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.54.3.182
